0 · The problem: sparse arithmetic does not guarantee cheap service

A mixture-of-experts language model buys parameter capacity by making only a small fraction of its feed-forward networks active for each token. Serving that model introduces a difficult separation: the work is sparse, the stored weights are large, and the destination of the work is decided at runtime. A dense layer has a predictable matrix shape and dataflow. An MoE layer has a distribution of matrix shapes, a changing communication graph, and a synchronization point at which the slowest participating device can delay everybody else.

The research objective is therefore more precise than “make MoE fast.” Given a trained checkpoint, a request distribution, an output-quality requirement, and a hardware budget, maximize completed useful work subject to latency constraints. For interactive serving, the constraints usually include time to first token (TTFT) and time per output token (TPOT), especially their tails. For offline generation, aggregate tokens per second may matter more. For a workstation, feasibility within GPU and host memory can dominate both. A technique optimized for one objective can be a poor answer to another.

max⁡θ  goodput(θ)Ctotal(θ)subject to Pr⁡(TTFT≤τfirst)≥qfirst,Pr⁡(TPOT≤τtoken)≥qtoken,Mr(θ)≤Cr,Qoutput≥Qrequiredθ={placement, batching, kernels, transport, admission}\begin{aligned}\max_\theta\;&\frac{\mathrm{goodput}(\theta)}{C_{\mathrm{total}}(\theta)}\\\text{subject to }&\Pr(\mathrm{TTFT}\le\tau_{\mathrm{first}})\ge q_{\mathrm{first}},\\&\Pr(\mathrm{TPOT}\le\tau_{\mathrm{token}})\ge q_{\mathrm{token}},\\&M_r(\theta)\le C_r,\quad Q_{\mathrm{output}}\ge Q_{\mathrm{required}}\\\theta&=\{\text{placement, batching, kernels, transport, admission}\}\end{aligned}θmax​subject to θ​Ctotal​(θ)goodput(θ)​Pr(TTFT≤τfirst​)≥qfirst​,Pr(TPOT≤τtoken​)≥qtoken​,Mr​(θ)≤Cr​,Qoutput​≥Qrequired​={placement, batching, kernels, transport, admission}​

This is an organizing model, not the exact optimization solved by every paper. It exposes the tradeoffs that disappear from isolated kernel speedups. Extra expert replicas can shorten a straggler but consume memory needed for concurrent KV caches. A larger batch can make expert matrix multiplication efficient while increasing the union of weights read and queueing delay. Moving experts to host memory can make a model fit while turning PCIe into the critical path. [7] [10] [13] [28]

The central thesis: MoE serving is the joint optimization of which weights must be resident, how many tokens reuse each weight load, where those tokens travel, and how long the slowest branch takes. Activated parameter count describes only part of this problem.

Three meanings of “efficient MoE”

First, model efficiency asks whether an MoE reaches a quality target with fewer activated FLOPs than a dense alternative. Second, execution efficiency asks how much of the hardware's attainable performance the irregular computation achieves. Third, service efficiency asks how many requests meet an SLO per unit of total cost. DeepSeekMoE primarily establishes an architectural quality–compute tradeoff; MegaBlocks studies sparse execution during training; MegaScale-Infer studies a serving architecture. These results complement one another, but their speedup denominators cannot be interchanged.

The guide first derives the tensors and costs, then follows the historical branches: routing and capacity; distributed execution; dropless kernels and imbalance; host offloading; fine-grained experts and specialized communication; and finally attention/expert disaggregation. Original paper figures are embedded beside their explanations. A figure that shows a conceptual tradeoff is identified as such; a measured plot is read with its workload and hardware conditions.

1 · Foundations: the layer, the batch, and the bottleneck

1.1 What an expert computes

Let a token representation be x∈R^d. A router computes E affinity scores and selects k logical experts. A common expert is a gated MLP with expansion width h; its gate and up projections are multiplied elementwise before a down projection. Shared experts, if present, run for every token. The precise activation, normalization of routing weights, shared-expert count, and selection rule are checkpoint properties.

r(x)=router⁡(x),S(x)=TopK⁡(r(x),k)fe(x)=Wdown,e[ϕ(Wgate,ex)⊙Wup,ex]y(x)=∑e∈S(x)ge(x)fe(x)+∑s∈sharedfs(x)Pexpert≈3dh,Fexpert/token≈6dhA=Tk,∑ene=Tk(ne=assignments to expert e)\begin{aligned}r(x)&=\operatorname{router}(x),\quad S(x)=\operatorname{TopK}(r(x),k)\\f_e(x)&=W_{\mathrm{down},e}[\phi(W_{\mathrm{gate},e}x)\odot W_{\mathrm{up},e}x]\\y(x)&=\sum_{e\in S(x)}g_e(x)f_e(x)+\sum_{s\in\mathrm{shared}}f_s(x)\\P_{\mathrm{expert}}&\approx3dh,\quad F_{\mathrm{expert/token}}\approx6dh\\A&=Tk,\quad\sum_e n_e=Tk\quad(n_e=\text{assignments to expert }e)\end{aligned}r(x)fe​(x)y(x)Pexpert​A​=router(x),S(x)=TopK(r(x),k)=Wdown,e​[ϕ(Wgate,e​x)⊙Wup,e​x]=e∈S(x)∑​ge​(x)fe​(x)+s∈shared∑​fs​(x)≈3dh,Fexpert/token​≈6dh=Tk,e∑​ne​=Tk(ne​=assignments to expert e)​

The parameter formula counts three weight matrices and omits small biases and metadata. It differs from the two-matrix FFNs in some early MoE papers. An “expert” is an MLP inside a layer, not a complete language model. Two experts with the same index in different layers have different parameters. An MoE with 64 experts and top-8 routing does not activate 8/64 of its attention, embeddings, normalization, or shared-expert computation. [3] [4] [5]

Prefill's T counts all scheduled prompt positions, potentially across chunked requests. Decode's T is usually the number of live sequence positions advanced in that step. Consequently, a service with 32 requests can give an expert thousands of tokens during prefill and only a few during decode. It is the per-expert n_e, rather than global batch size alone, that determines the matrix shape seen by an expert kernel.

Derivation: what gradient does a sparse router actually receive?

Set up the exact gate convention. For one token x, let fₑ(x) be expert e's output and zₑ(x) its router logit. First assume a fixed selected set S and a softmax renormalized only over S. The selected set is locally constant away from top-k ties. Treat the expert outputs as fixed while differentiating router logits.

ge=eze∑j∈Sezj,y=∑e∈Sgefe∂ge∂zj=ge(1[e=j]−gj),j∈S∂y∂zj=∑e∈Sfege(1[e=j]−gj)=gjfj−gj∑e∈Sgefe=gj(fj−y)∂L∂zj=gj(∇yL)⊤(fj−y)\begin{aligned}g_e&=\frac{e^{z_e}}{\sum_{j\in S}e^{z_j}},\quad y=\sum_{e\in S}g_ef_e\\\frac{\partial g_e}{\partial z_j}&=g_e(\mathbf1[e=j]-g_j),\quad j\in S\\\frac{\partial y}{\partial z_j}&=\sum_{e\in S}f_eg_e(\mathbf1[e=j]-g_j)\\&=g_jf_j-g_j\sum_{e\in S}g_ef_e=g_j(f_j-y)\\\frac{\partial L}{\partial z_j}&=g_j(\nabla_yL)^\top(f_j-y)\end{aligned}ge​∂zj​∂ge​​∂zj​∂y​∂zj​∂L​​=∑j∈S​ezj​eze​​,y=e∈S∑​ge​fe​=ge​(1[e=j]−gj​),j∈S=e∈S∑​fe​ge​(1[e=j]−gj​)=gj​fj​−gj​e∈S∑​ge​fe​=gj​(fj​−y)=gj​(∇y​L)⊤(fj​−y)​

Interpret each term. The expert receives credit relative to the current weighted output. Increasing a logit is useful when moving toward that expert decreases the downstream loss. Unselected logits have zero local derivative through this renormalized gate because they do not occur in its denominator. The discrete change of S at a ranking boundary is not captured by this derivative.

An instructive degeneracy: if k=1 and the selected weight is renormalized to one, then fⱼ=y and the local router gradient above is zero. A top-1 router therefore needs another path for learning routing—such as retaining the selected expert's probability from the full softmax, an auxiliary objective, noise/relaxations, or an estimator. Switch's selected probability convention must not be replaced by this renormalized gate without changing training.

For full-softmax probabilities p over all experts followed by selection without renormalizing, y=Σₑ∈S pₑfₑ. Differentiation instead gives ∂y/∂zⱼ=1[j∈S]pⱼfⱼ−pⱼy, including a denominator effect for unselected j. This is why two pieces of code both described as “top-k MoE” can have different gradients and output scales. Neither calculation differentiates through a hard sorting decision at a tie.

Exercise — A two-expert gate

Let S={1,2}, f₁=2, f₂=−1, and g₁=0.75, g₂=0.25. Compute y and ∂y/∂z₁ under selected-set renormalization. What happens at k=1?

Show worked solution
y=0.75⋅2+0.25(−1)=1.25∂y∂z1=0.75(2−1.25)=0.5625\begin{aligned}y&=0.75\cdot2+0.25(-1)=1.25\\\frac{\partial y}{\partial z_1}&=0.75(2-1.25)=0.5625\end{aligned}y∂z1​∂y​​=0.75⋅2+0.25(−1)=1.25=0.75(2−1.25)=0.5625​

For one selected expert, g₁=1 and y=f₁, hence the derivative is zero away from a selection boundary. This does not imply that every implemented top-1 router has zero gradient: the full-softmax, nonrenormalized convention above is different.

1.2 Storage, FLOPs, and actual weight traffic

For equal experts, total expert storage scales with E, arithmetic per token with k, and weight reads per batch with the number U of distinct experts touched. These are three different quantities. Suppose each token selects k distinct experts uniformly and token selections are independent. An expert is absent from one token with probability 1−k/E and absent from a B-token batch with probability (1−k/E)^B. Summing the indicator that each expert is used gives:

E[U(B)]=E[1−(1−kE)B]E[ne]=BkEVexpert weights≈U(B)Wexpert\begin{aligned}\mathbb E[U(B)]&=E\left[1-\left(1-\frac kE\right)^B\right]\\\mathbb E[n_e]&=\frac{Bk}{E}\\V_{\mathrm{expert\ weights}}&\approx U(B)W_{\mathrm{expert}}\end{aligned}E[U(B)]E[ne​]Vexpert weights​​=E[1−(1−Ek​)B]=EBk​≈U(B)Wexpert​​

For E=8, k=2, B=8, the expected union is about 7.20 experts. Per-token sparsity remains 75%, but nearly all expert weights participate somewhere in the batch. Conversely, the same weight can now serve several tokens, improving reuse. Batching simultaneously weakens the weight-skipping benefit and strengthens matrix efficiency. It does not “turn the model dense” in FLOPs: only Bk assignments are still evaluated. This distinction is essential to understanding both disaggregation and approximate batch-aware expert reduction. [27] [28]

This occupancy model assumes each token selects k distinct experts uniformly. It does not model skew, expert replication, or a real GEMM kernel.

The model above is illustrative. Real routing has domain dependence, token correlation, layer dependence, and shared experts. The correct measurement is a distribution: U, each n_e, the maximum per-rank load, and their changes across requests. A mean activation frequency cannot describe a service whose coding and multilingual traffic activate different experts.

Derivation: why token sparsity disappears in the batch’s weight set

Assumptions. Each of B independent tokens selects a uniformly random k-element subset of E experts, without replacement within a token. Expert choices for one token are dependent; token-to-token choices are independent. Let Iₑ be one if expert e is used by at least one token, and U=Σₑ Iₑ.

p=kE,Pr⁡(one token avoids e)=E−kE=1−pPr⁡(all B tokens avoid e)=(1−p)BE[Ie]=1−(1−p)BE[U]=∑eE[Ie]=E[1−(1−kE)B]\begin{aligned}p&=\frac kE,\quad\Pr(\text{one token avoids }e)=\frac{E-k}E=1-p\\\Pr(\text{all }B\text{ tokens avoid }e)&=(1-p)^B\\\mathbb E[I_e]&=1-(1-p)^B\\\mathbb E[U]&=\sum_e\mathbb E[I_e]=E\left[1-\left(1-\frac kE\right)^B\right]\end{aligned}pPr(all B tokens avoid e)E[Ie​]E[U]​=Ek​,Pr(one token avoids e)=EE−k​=1−p=(1−p)B=1−(1−p)B=e∑​E[Ie​]=E[1−(1−Ek​)B]​

Linearity of expectation needs no independence between Iₑ values. The independence assumption enters only when multiplying the B avoidance probabilities. For nonuniform independent routing with marginal pₑ, the general result is Σₑ[1−(1−pₑ)^B]. Correlated requests can violate even this product.

Expected assignments per expert are Bk/E, but expected distinct experts is a different statistic. An expert touched once and an expert touched 100 times each contribute one to U. This separates transferred weight bytes from expert FLOPs.

E[Vweights]≈WexpertE[U]Fgated≈6dhBkIamortized≈6dhBk3dhswE[U]=2BkswE[U]\begin{aligned}\mathbb E[V_{\mathrm{weights}}]&\approx W_{\mathrm{expert}}\mathbb E[U]\\F_{\mathrm{gated}}&\approx6dhBk\\I_{\mathrm{amortized}}&\approx\frac{6dhBk}{3dh s_w\mathbb E[U]}=\frac{2Bk}{s_w\mathbb E[U]}\end{aligned}E[Vweights​]Fgated​Iamortized​​≈Wexpert​E[U]≈6dhBk≈3dhsw​E[U]6dhBk​=sw​E[U]2Bk​​

At tiny B, U≈Bk and intensity≈2/s_w; at large B, U approaches E and weight reuse grows approximately with Bk/E. Sparse arithmetic survives: Bk assignments are still far below BE unless k≈E. The same batch can touch nearly every weight while executing only a fraction of all token–expert pairs.

For a desired expected touched fraction η, solve 1−(1−k/E)^B≥η. Taking logarithms gives B≥log(1−η)/log(1−k/E), with the inequality direction handled because the denominator is negative. This locates a workload-dependent weight-union crossover rather than a universal batch threshold.

For E=8 and k=2, what smallest integer B gives at least 90% expected expert coverage? How many assignments occur then?

B≥log⁡0.1log⁡0.75≈8.004,Bmin⁡=9E[U]=8(1−0.759)≈7.3993A=Bk=18,Adense=BE=72\begin{aligned}B&\ge\frac{\log0.1}{\log0.75}\approx8.004,\quad B_{\min}=9\\\mathbb E[U]&=8(1-0.75^9)\approx7.3993\\A&=Bk=18,\quad A_{\mathrm{dense}}=BE=72\end{aligned}BE[U]A​≥log0.75log0.1​≈8.004,Bmin​=9=8(1−0.759)≈7.3993=Bk=18,Adense​=BE=72​
