1.3 Derive the expert roofline

Let s_w be effective bytes per stored weight, including amortized scales if needed. If one expert's weights are read once for n_e tokens and activation traffic is relatively small, its arithmetic intensity is approximately 2n_e/s_w FLOP/byte. This gives a useful lower bound, not a runtime prediction:

Fe≈6dhne,We≈3dhswIe≈FeWe=2neswte≥max⁡(FeCeffective(shape),WeβHBM)\begin{aligned}F_e&\approx6dh n_e,\quad W_e\approx3dh s_w\\I_e&\approx\frac{F_e}{W_e}=\frac{2n_e}{s_w}\\t_e&\ge\max\left(\frac{F_e}{C_{\mathrm{effective}}(\mathrm{shape})},\frac{W_e}{\beta_{\mathrm{HBM}}}\right)\end{aligned}Fe​Ie​te​​≈6dhne​,We​≈3dhsw​≈We​Fe​​=sw​2ne​​≥max(Ceffective​(shape)Fe​​,βHBM​We​​)​

At BF16, s_w=2, so I_e≈n_e. An expert receiving two decode tokens has a very different balance from one receiving 512 prompt tokens. The “effective” compute rate must be shape dependent: a tiny matrix cannot be assumed to reach the dense peak. Quantization reduces weight bytes, but conversion, scale loads, alignment, and supported tile sizes affect the realized gain. Multiple experts may share one grouped launch, yet this does not mathematically merge their distinct weights into one reusable matrix.

For d=4,096 and h=14,336, a gated expert has 176,160,768 weights. BF16 storage is about 352 MB in decimal units, while one expert call for one token costs about 352 million FLOPs. At an illustrative 25 GB/s effective host-to-device bandwidth, transferring that expert alone takes at least 14.1 ms. Its input and output vectors total only about 16 KB. This large ratio motivates Fiddler's choice to sometimes move the activation to the CPU rather than move the weight to the GPU. It does not prove CPU execution is faster: CPU compute and DRAM time still enter the comparison.

1.4 A layer is a distributed dependency graph

The router produces token-to-expert assignments; a packing/permutation step groups them by destination; dispatch transfers them; local expert kernels run; combine transfers results back; an inverse permutation and weighted reduction restore token order. A top-k token may be copied k times, but hierarchical transports can reuse a token payload when several selected experts share a node.

tlayer≈tgate+pack+tdispatch+max⁡rtexperts,r+tcombine+unpack(without useful overlap)Vdispatch+return≈2Tkdsa,Vremote≈2Tkdsafremote\begin{aligned}t_{\mathrm{layer}}&\approx t_{\mathrm{gate+pack}}+t_{\mathrm{dispatch}}+\max_r t_{\mathrm{experts},r}+t_{\mathrm{combine+unpack}}\\&\text{(without useful overlap)}\\V_{\mathrm{dispatch+return}}&\approx2Tkds_a,\quad V_{\mathrm{remote}}\approx2Tkds_a f_{\mathrm{remote}}\end{aligned}tlayer​Vdispatch+return​​≈tgate+pack​+tdispatch​+rmax​texperts,r​+tcombine+unpack​(without useful overlap)≈2Tkdsa​,Vremote​≈2Tkdsa​fremote​​

This byte estimate excludes routing indices, scales, headers, padding, and duplicated transmissions. For small messages, latency and synchronization can dominate bandwidth. For large messages, link utilization, bisection bandwidth, and congestion become central. A kernel that finishes quickly on seven ranks is irrelevant if an eighth rank determines completion. Model the critical path before adding individual kernel speedups. [8] [10]

2 · 2017–2021: conditional capacity creates a routing problem

Problems and objectives. Conditional computation promises more parameters without activating every parameter for every token, but it creates unequal expert loads. This period establishes sparse routing and distributed expert ownership while confronting the coupled problems of learning useful specialization, preventing collapse, and fitting irregular token assignments into bounded execution buffers.

2.1 Sparse gates, GShard, and Switch

Core idea. Sparse gates select only a few experts per token; GShard scales this idea through distributed expert execution, and Switch simplifies routing to one expert per token. The common strategy grows total capacity while bounding activated computation, leaving balancing and overflow as explicit design problems.

Shazeer and colleagues established the sparse-gated layer as a route to large parameter capacity: only selected experts receive a token, and auxiliary objectives encourage useful load distribution. GShard combined top-2 routing with a scalable partitioning system. Switch then made a decisive simplification: select one expert per token. Top-1 reduces duplicate dispatch and expert work, but creates a sharper dependence on the chosen expert and on training stability. The architecture change reduces the work graph before the system tries to optimize it. [1] [2] [3]

Read Switch's figure from bottom to top. Self-attention first produces token representations. The router then sends the two example tokens to different FFNs. The dotted path carries the router probability used to scale the selected result; the other FFNs exist as stored capacity but perform no computation for that token. The residual path remains. This explains why missing a routed expert is not equivalent to skipping an arbitrary unused branch: the selected branch contributes a learned function to the output.

2.2 Capacity factor: the original regularity compromise

Early accelerator-friendly implementations allocate an equal-size buffer for every expert. For top-1 routing over T tokens, a common capacity is C=ceil(cT/E), where c is the capacity factor. For top-k the convention must account for assignments, often C≈ceil(cTk/E). Some implementations define c differently, so the actual allocation rule should be inspected rather than inferred from a configuration label.

Nslots=ECNpadding=∑emax⁡(C−ne,0)Noverflow=∑emax⁡(ne−C,0)ne=actual assignments to expert e\begin{aligned}N_{\mathrm{slots}}&=EC\\N_{\mathrm{padding}}&=\sum_e\max(C-n_e,0)\\N_{\mathrm{overflow}}&=\sum_e\max(n_e-C,0)\\n_e&=\text{actual assignments to expert }e\end{aligned}Nslots​Npadding​Noverflow​ne​​=EC=e∑​max(C−ne​,0)=e∑​max(ne​−C,0)=actual assignments to expert e​

Read the two halves of the capacity figure together. At factor 1.0, one expert's bucket overflows while another still has spare room. Spare capacity at the wrong expert cannot execute the overflowing expert's function. Increasing the factor to 1.5 creates more room everywhere, admitting the previously dropped assignment but also allocating unused slots elsewhere. The issue is a mismatch between dynamic semantic routing and fixed accelerator buffers, not a lack of total token slots in the abstract.

Dropping overflow during training bypasses an expert contribution according to the model's prescribed rule. Increasing inference capacity can avoid that loss, at a memory and kernel cost. A serving engine must not silently introduce new dropping merely because a buffer was sized for the average load. “Dropless” means all selected assignments are processed; it does not mean zero padding, zero permutation, or equal completion time.

Derivation: capacity, overflow probability, and the price of padding

A probabilistic model, not a routing guarantee. Under the independent uniform model, the load Xₑ of one expert across N tokens is Binomial(N,k/E). Therefore μ=Nk/E and variance μ(1−k/E). A fixed-capacity kernel with C slots per expert reserves EC assignments even when only Nk are useful. For C≈cμ, the assignment-slot utilization is approximately 1/c if no tokens are dropped and padding is executed.

A capacity factor by itself says nothing about the probability of overflow until a load model is given. For any nonnegative t, Markov's inequality applied to exp(tXₑ) gives:

Pr⁡(Xe≥C)≤e−tCE[etXe]=e−tC(1−p+pet)N≤exp⁡[−tC+μ(et−1)]\begin{aligned}\Pr(X_e\ge C)&\le e^{-tC}\mathbb E[e^{tX_e}]\\&=e^{-tC}(1-p+pe^t)^N\\&\le\exp[-tC+\mu(e^t-1)]\end{aligned}Pr(Xe​≥C)​≤e−tCE[etXe​]=e−tC(1−p+pet)N≤exp[−tC+μ(et−1)]​

The final step uses 1+u≤exp(u). Set C=(1+δ)μ and choose exp(t)=1+δ, which minimizes this upper bound. Then:

Pr⁡(Xe≥(1+δ)μ)≤[eδ(1+δ)1+δ]μPr⁡(any expert overflows)≤E[eδ(1+δ)1+δ]μ\begin{aligned}\Pr(X_e\ge(1+\delta)\mu)&\le\left[\frac{e^\delta}{(1+\delta)^{1+\delta}}\right]^\mu\\\Pr(\text{any expert overflows})&\le E\left[\frac{e^\delta}{(1+\delta)^{1+\delta}}\right]^\mu\end{aligned}Pr(Xe​≥(1+δ)μ)Pr(any expert overflows)​≤[(1+δ)1+δeδ​]μ≤E[(1+δ)1+δeδ​]μ​

The second line is a union bound, so it does not require expert loads to be mutually independent. Bounds can be loose; cap them at one. Exact binomial tails or measured router traces can give a better sizing estimate. The derivation explains why the same capacity factor is less reliable at small per-expert token counts: relative fluctuations are roughly 1/√μ.

Dropless kernels replace a quality risk from dropping with an execution-shape problem. With tile granularity T, a block-sparse implementation may execute Σₑ T ceil(Xₑ/T) slots, whose excess over Nk is less than ET across nonempty experts. This is not zero padding; it is bounded tile padding instead of a globally chosen expert capacity. During decode, Xₑ can be tiny compared with T, making the distinction decisive.

Exercise — Compare two kinds of padding

Four experts receive loads (1,1,1,13). Compare a capacity-16 batched kernel with a dropless kernel using tiles of four token rows. Count slots, useful-slot fractions, and whether either drops tokens.

Show worked solution

The fixed-capacity kernel executes 4·16=64 slots for 16 assignments: 25% useful. The tiled kernel executes 4+4+4+16=28 slots: 16/28≈57.14% useful. Neither drops an assignment. Dropless does not mean padding-free: its 12 extra slots remain a real cost. The result does not imply equal per-slot efficiency for the two kernels.

2.3 Load balancing has both a learning and a systems meaning

Core idea. Switch-style auxiliary losses use assignment frequencies and router probabilities to discourage expert collapse during learning. Expert Choice reverses the allocation direction by giving experts fixed token buckets, changing routing semantics as well as the balance constraint.

A representative Switch-style auxiliary loss multiplies the fraction of tokens assigned to each expert by its mean router probability, then sums over experts. The hard assignment statistic measures actual selection; the soft statistic supplies gradients to the router. This discourages collapse, but its batch-level optimum is not a guarantee of balanced future inference traffic. The data mixture, batch size, and deployment domain can all change.

fe=1T∑t1[e selected for t](top-1)Pe=1T∑tpe(xt)Lbalance=αE∑efePe\begin{aligned}f_e&=\frac1T\sum_t\mathbf1[e\text{ selected for }t]\quad\text{(top-1)}\\P_e&=\frac1T\sum_t p_e(x_t)\\L_{\mathrm{balance}}&=\alpha E\sum_e f_eP_e\end{aligned}fe​Pe​Lbalance​​=T1​t∑​1[e selected for t](top-1)=T1​t∑​pe​(xt​)=αEe∑​fe​Pe​​

Making the balancing penalty arbitrarily large is not free. It can force tokens toward experts that are less useful for the task. Expert Choice changes the allocation viewpoint: experts choose a fixed number of tokens, producing balanced expert buckets but a variable number of experts per token. This is an architecture/training alternative, not a transparent replacement for a fixed top-k autoregressive checkpoint. Serving papers must therefore distinguish changing routing to improve balance from executing the same routing more evenly through replication or placement. [23] [8]

3 · 2021–2022: distributed execution becomes the problem

Problems and objectives. Once experts span devices, sparse FLOPs stop predicting execution time: dispatch, congestion, idle ranks, and incompatible parallelism choices can dominate. These systems expose expert work to schedulers and choose communication and parallelism plans around its irregular dependency graph.

3.1 FastMoE and FasterMoE: expose and schedule the irregular work

Core idea. FastMoE exposes expert-parallel execution in a general framework; FasterMoE adds mechanisms such as dynamic expert shadowing and finer scheduling to mitigate hotspots and overlap work. Its optional routing changes must be distinguished from optimizations that execute unchanged assignments.

FastMoE made expert-parallel execution accessible in a general GPU training stack. FasterMoE identified three interacting costs: changing expert load, coarse synchronous execution, and all-to-all congestion. Its dynamic shadowing replicates selected expert work to reduce hotspots; its finer schedule overlaps operations; an optional expert-selection change addresses congestion when changing the model's routing is allowed. These are different guarantees and should remain separate in a serving design. The published speedups are training results and do not by themselves establish decode latency. [21] [22]

The lasting lesson is that an MoE layer need not be one indivisible “all-to-all, then all experts, then all-to-all” operation. It can be split into tasks with dependencies. However, the scheduler must expose enough independent work without making every matrix so small that launch and tile inefficiency dominate. This balance reappears in Tutel, Lina, DeepEP, and disaggregated serving.

3.2 DeepSpeed-MoE: use different parallelism for different parameter classes

Core idea. Assign different combinations of tensor, expert, and data parallelism to expert and non-expert parameters, and coordinate their communication. This avoids imposing one parallelism degree on operators with different storage and execution needs.

Tensor parallelism splits the matrices of one operator; expert parallelism assigns different experts to different devices; data parallelism replicates a function across different inputs. Expert slicing is tensor partitioning inside an expert. DeepSpeed-MoE's important insight is that expert and non-expert parameters have different optimal combinations of these dimensions. Forcing one tensor-parallel degree onto both can either replicate too many expert weights or over-communicate attention. [7]

Read the expanded boxes independently. The non-expert block uses tensor slices within a group and data-parallel replicas across groups. The expert block uses expert ownership plus slices of individual experts. The labels in the original example describe a 16-GPU arrangement with eight experts; they are not a universal deployment recipe. Arrows marked all-reduce, all-gather, and all-to-all correspond to different mathematical obligations: sum partial matrix outputs, assemble required shards, and exchange token assignments.

For a two-layer MLP, a column split of the first weight matrix produces independent hidden slices. A matching row split of the second matrix produces partial output vectors that must be summed. Splitting an expert further may allow its weights to fit and its busy batch to run faster, but adds a collective on the expert path. By contrast, putting different complete experts on different ranks avoids that within-expert reduction and requires token dispatch. The optimal choice depends on expert width, n_e, network topology, and memory.

DeepSpeed-MoE also uses hierarchical all-to-all: organize transfers to exploit faster links within a node and reduce expensive cross-node exchanges. Parallelism-coordinated communication avoids moving redundant copies created by other parallel dimensions. The general rule is to identify which ranks contain identical token information before multiplying the traffic estimate by every tensor-parallel rank.

3.3 Architecture compression is a separate part of the DeepSpeed contribution

Core idea. PR-MoE changes how expert capacity is distributed across depth and adds a residual dense path; Mixture-of-Students distills a shallower model. These reduce the model being executed, so their gains are distinct from faster execution of an unchanged checkpoint.

PR-MoE varies expert capacity across depth and combines a residual dense branch with sparse expert computation; Mixture-of-Students reduces depth through a staged distillation recipe. These can reduce the model being served. They are not simply faster kernels for the same checkpoint. The original report includes both system-only comparisons and comparisons that combine a smaller quality-matched model with the system. Its largest model equivalence is partly projected from scaling observations; a careful reader should check which accuracy equivalence was actually measured. [7]

This distinction matters when using a headline such as “7.3× faster.” Ask whether the numerator and denominator execute the same model, different models at a measured quality target, or different models with projected quality. All three can be useful experiments, but they support different conclusions.

4 · 2022–2023: Tutel and the problem of changing execution shapes

Problems and objectives. The best execution plan depends on the changing number of tokens assigned to experts, yet changing layouts can itself require expensive migration. Tutel addresses how to switch among equivalent parallel execution plans cheaply and partition work so useful communication/computation overlap remains possible.

4.1 Why one parallelism plan is insufficient

Core idea. Tutel builds equivalent execution plans around compatible parameter layouts and selects among them according to workload shape. Capacity-axis pipelining and specialized routing kernels complement the plan selection by reducing communication and indexing overhead.

Tutel starts from an awkward observation: the amount of work assigned to an MoE layer changes over time, and the best execution plan changes with it. A plan that reduces communication may replicate computation; a plan that reduces computation may require gathering weights or activations. If changing the plan first requires migrating a large parameter tensor, the switch can cost more than it saves. Tutel therefore constructs mathematically equivalent execution paths that share a compatible parameter layout. [8]

Its adaptive parallelism parameter moves between data-parallel behavior and combinations of expert, data, and model parallelism. The paper's “zero-cost switching” refers to avoiding substantial parameter/token migration caused by changing layouts; it does not assert that any chosen execution path has zero communication or that runtime profiling is free. A dictionary maps workload-capacity ranges to a preferred parallelism, pipeline degree, and all-to-all algorithm.

4.2 Partition the expert-capacity axis, not arbitrary requests

Naively splitting a batch can worsen imbalance: a globally balanced batch may split into small chunks that each activate only a few experts. Tutel partitions the dispatched capacity dimension so each pipeline stage has an expert-aligned chunk. Communication and expert computation for different chunks can then overlap on separate streams.

Follow a single color through the diagram. E denotes an expert destination and C denotes a capacity partition. The first rearrangement splits each expert's work into C₀ and C₁; the following all-to-all delivers those partitions to their owners. An expert can compute one partition while another is being transferred. The second exchange reverses ownership and the final merge restores the expected layout. The graphic is about data organization that permits overlap, not a claim that independent CUDA streams automatically overlap well.

For m chunks with stage times d, c, and r, an ideal pipeline resembles fill time plus (m−1) times the slowest stage. But d, c, and r themselves depend on chunk size. Smaller chunks increase launch counts and reduce matrix efficiency; more concurrent communication can contend for the same SMs or links. Tutel jointly considers pipeline degree and transport choice rather than optimizing each in isolation.

4.3 Encode/decode overhead and two-dimensional communication

A literal implementation of routing can construct a large dense dispatch tensor and express scatter/gather as matrix multiplication. That uses general primitives for a sparse indexing operation. Tutel's fast encode/decode kernels use expert indices and slot locations directly, reducing both temporary storage and non-expert overhead. This is especially important when expert GEMMs are already small: shaving the GEMM while leaving repeated reshapes and routing launches untouched can give little end-to-end benefit.

Its two-dimensional hierarchical all-to-all reorganizes data across local and inter-node communication dimensions, aggregating messages to improve network use. Aggregation has a cost, so it does not dominate a direct exchange at every message size. Tutel's training and vision-MoE evaluations establish the value of adaptation in their workloads; contemporary LLM decode still needs its own shape and latency measurements. [8]

5 · 2022–2023: MegaBlocks removes the drop-or-pad dilemma

Problems and objectives. Fixed-capacity expert batches either waste arithmetic on padding or lose assignments through dropping. This branch asks whether variable expert loads can be represented directly as schedulable matrix structure, preserving every assignment while retaining GPU-friendly tiles.

5.1 Turn the routing pattern into matrix structure

Core idea. MegaBlocks permutes token assignments by expert and expresses unequal expert batches as dynamically structured block-sparse matrix operations. Scheduling occupied tiles preserves assignments while limiting padding to tile granularity.

The original fixed-capacity representation can execute every expert as an equal-shaped batched GEMM. Unfortunately, equal shape comes from padding underloaded experts or dropping overloaded assignments. MegaBlocks instead expresses the entire expert computation as a dynamically shaped block-sparse matrix operation. Tokens are permuted into expert groups; each group multiplies only its expert's weights. The structure resembles a block diagonal matrix with unequal-height diagonal regions. [9]

Read panels A→B→C as equivalent algebra with progressively better representation. A uses separate equally sized expert batches. B places those batches into a block-diagonal output. C subdivides the diagonal regions into fixed tiles, allowing different experts to occupy different numbers of tile rows. White regions do not represent a dense matrix that is calculated and masked afterward; they are work that the sparse kernel does not schedule.

Xe=(PX)rows assigned to eHe=ϕ(XeWup,e),Ye=HeWdown,eY=inverse_permute_and_weight⁡({Ye},g)Nallocated=∑eb⌈neb⌉,Npadding<EactivebTwo-matrix illustration; P orders expanded assignments by expert.\begin{aligned}X_e&=(PX)_{\mathrm{rows\ assigned\ to}\ e}\\H_e&=\phi(X_eW_{\mathrm{up},e}),\quad Y_e=H_eW_{\mathrm{down},e}\\Y&=\operatorname{inverse\_permute\_and\_weight}(\{Y_e\},g)\\N_{\mathrm{allocated}}&=\sum_e b\left\lceil\frac{n_e}b\right\rceil,\quad N_{\mathrm{padding}}<E_{\mathrm{active}}b\\&\text{Two-matrix illustration; }P\text{ orders expanded assignments by expert.}\end{aligned}Xe​He​YNallocated​​=(PX)rows assigned to e​=ϕ(Xe​Wup,e​),Ye​=He​Wdown,e​=inverse_permute_and_weight({Ye​},g)=e∑​b⌈bne​​⌉,Npadding​<Eactive​bTwo-matrix illustration; P orders expanded assignments by expert.​

The tile bound differs from padding every expert to the largest n_e. It is also not zero padding: the original implementation rounds expert batches to a block multiple, using 128×128 sparsity blocks. The authors explicitly target expert batches with thousands or tens of thousands of tokens. If a decode expert receives one or two tokens, blindly inheriting a 128-row padding choice can destroy efficiency. This is why the conceptual breakthrough transfers to inference while the original training configuration does not automatically transfer.

Derivation: dispatch and combine are a gather–scatter algebra

Let X∈ℝ^(N×d) hold token rows and let M=Nk be the number of assignments. Construct a dispatch matrix D∈{0,1}^(M×N), one row per assignment: Dₐᵢ=1 exactly when assignment a comes from token i. Each row has one nonzero; each token column has k. Sorting assignments by expert is a permutation P, so the packed expert input is Z=PDX.

The block-diagonal operator F applies each expert to only its own rows. It is usually nonlinear, so F is an operator here, not one fixed matrix. Let G be diagonal with the original gate weight attached to each packed assignment. The combined output is:

Z=PDXY=D⊤P⊤GF(Z)\begin{aligned}Z&=PDX\\Y&=D^\top P^\top G F(Z)\end{aligned}ZY​=PDX=D⊤P⊤GF(Z)​

D duplicates token rows; Dᵀ sums assignment outputs back into token rows. P changes execution order and Pᵀ restores it. This equation makes three correctness requirements explicit: assignment identity must survive communication, gate weights must follow the same permutation, and combine must sum all selected contributions exactly once.

Backward operations follow from inner products. If Z=AX, then ⟨∇ZL,A·δX⟩=⟨Aᵀ∇ZL,δX⟩, hence ∇XL=Aᵀ∇ZL. Dispatch's backward therefore sums gradients from duplicated assignments. Combine's backward broadcasts a token's output gradient to its assignments and multiplies by their gate weights, with separate gradients for G if gates train. This explains why a gather in the forward path pairs with a scatter-add in the backward path.

Sparse kernels and communication libraries implement these identities using indices, offsets and buffers, never dense D or P. Changing the packing order is exact if the inverse and weights are changed consistently. Dropping an assignment, clipping an expert's capacity, or substituting an expert changes the operator itself. Reduced communication from such a change must be assessed together with its quality consequences.

Exercise — A missing inverse permutation

Token 1 selects A with weight 0.2 and B with 0.8; token 2 selects A with 0.6 and B with 0.4. Packed order is (1A,2A,1B,2B). What gate vector belongs in G, and why is (0.2,0.8,0.6,0.4) wrong?

Show worked solution

The matching gate vector is (0.2,0.6,0.8,0.4). The alternative keeps token-major weights while expert outputs are expert-major, swapping token 2's A weight with token 1's B weight. If every expert output were the same scalar one, the wrong combination would produce 0.8 for token 1 and 1.2 for token 2 instead of one each. This is a direct correctness test independent of any model benchmark.

5.2 Why sparse metadata and transposition matter

The first projection has a sparse output topology; the second consumes a sparse intermediate. The backward pass requires additional transposed variants. Generic sparse libraries may assume a fixed topology, require expensive preprocessing, or lack one needed multiply. MoE routing changes at every invocation, so precomputed metadata can become invalid immediately.

MegaBlocks combines block-row offsets and column indices with explicit row indices, allowing a GPU thread block to locate its assigned nonzero tile directly. A secondary transpose index permits traversal in the opposite order without copying the entire sparse payload. The extra metadata is small relative to a tile's thousands of elements. This is a recurring systems principle: spend a few bytes of index metadata to avoid moving a much larger activation tensor. [9]

5.3 Grouped GEMM is the related inference path

A grouped GEMM launch receives many matrix problems with different row counts and schedules their tiles together. It reduces per-expert launch overhead and exposes work from several experts to the GPU. It still has to account for empty experts, unequal matrix sizes, alignment, quantization scales, and output offsets. Block-sparse algebra and grouped GEMM are related representations of irregular expert work; they are not synonyms.

DeepGEMM distinguishes contiguous grouped layouts useful for throughput-oriented processing from masked layouts useful when small expert batches occupy reserved regions. Its exact APIs evolve, so inspect the deployed revision. The durable design question is whether the kernel can process the actual n_e distribution without excessive padding or launch overhead, while preserving scale and permutation semantics. The original MegaBlocks “up to 40% over Tutel” result is training evidence; the inference decision requires measured decode kernels. [16] [9]

6 · 2023 onward: Lina, replica placement, and the slowest rank

Problems and objectives. A layer completes only when its slowest required expert work returns, so average utilization can hide damaging hotspots. The focus shifts to scheduling and physical replication that reduce the busiest rank’s load while accounting for shared communication resources and changing routing distributions.

6.1 Imbalance is a tail problem

Lina separates two causes of all-to-all delay. During training, all-to-all needed by the current MoE layer can compete with gradient all-reduce from other work. During inference, skewed expert popularity creates unequal compute and traffic, making the collective wait for overloaded destinations. Solving one does not automatically solve the other. [10]

The chart compares training and inference popularity, not expert quality. Blue bars are relatively balanced under the training regime; orange outlines show that deployment inputs can concentrate assignments. The two panels use four and sixteen experts. The tallest orange bar determines work on a hotspot, while low bars represent potential idle capacity. A balanced number of experts per GPU cannot fix this if the experts have different popularity.

A simple imbalance factor is max_r A_r divided by the mean rank assignment count. It is useful but incomplete: two ranks with identical assignments can still differ because one executes many tiny expert matrices, uses a slower link, or misses its expert cache. A better predictor sums shape-dependent expert runtimes and communication on each rank, then evaluates the maximum.

6.2 Lina's two-stage inference scheduler

Core idea. Lina predicts upcoming expert popularity from earlier routing paths to prepare replica placement, then corrects the plan when actual gate decisions arrive. This moves resource preparation ahead of the dependency while preserving the true expert choices.

Lina profiles correlations between the expert path already taken by a token and likely experts in a later layer. It estimates aggregate popularity early, before the next layer's true gate results are available, and uses that estimate to prepare a resource allocation. Popular experts receive more replicas; less popular experts can be packed together. Once the real routing decisions arrive, the scheduler checks whether the important experts differ enough to require correction.

The prediction is used to prepare resources, not to declare the predicted expert output semantically interchangeable with the true selected expert. Prediction error can therefore cost scheduling or movement without necessarily changing the model's routing. This distinction contrasts with SiDA's replacement of routing by an independently predicted table. Lina also partitions communications into smaller operations so urgent all-to-all can be prioritized over concurrent all-reduce and overlapped with expert work. [10]

There is a cost to this adaptability. A prediction must arrive early enough; replicas need storage; moving weights is expensive; and the placement needs an unambiguous version while tokens are in flight. A policy that reacts to every small fluctuation can spend more time migrating than it recovers from better balance. The important timescale is the persistence of the load pattern relative to migration and measurement delay.

6.3 EPLB: logical experts versus physical copies

Core idea. Map each logical expert to one or more physical replicas and distribute its assignments among those copies. Rebalancing physical placement can reduce hot-rank load without changing which logical expert the router selected.

Modern expert load balancing makes a clean distinction between E logical experts in the checkpoint and R physical slots across devices. Several slots may contain identical copies of one logical expert. The router still chooses the logical expert; a second mapping chooses which physical replica handles the assignment. This preserves the intended computation provided the copies, numerical mode, and combination rule are consistent. [17]

re≥1,∑ere≤R,λper replica,e≈λeremin⁡replicas,placement  max⁡r∑a∈replicas on rW^asubject to weight-memory and communication-locality constraintsλe=predicted assignments to logical expert e\begin{aligned}r_e&\ge1,\quad\sum_e r_e\le R,\quad\lambda_{\mathrm{per\ replica},e}\approx\frac{\lambda_e}{r_e}\\\min_{\mathrm{replicas,placement}}\;&\max_r\sum_{a\in\mathrm{replicas\ on}\ r}\widehat W_a\\\text{subject to }&\text{weight-memory and communication-locality constraints}\\\lambda_e&=\text{predicted assignments to logical expert }e\end{aligned}re​replicas,placementmin​subject to λe​​≥1,e∑​re​≤R,λper replica,e​≈re​λe​​rmax​a∈replicas on r∑​Wa​weight-memory and communication-locality constraints=predicted assignments to logical expert e​

If all experts have equal weight size and linear work per assignment, λ_e/r_e suggests allocating more copies to busy experts. Real implementations add integer constraints, node groups, expert groups, and non-linear kernel efficiency. Splitting a hot expert across too many replicas can make every local matrix inefficient. Minimizing assignment imbalance is therefore an approximation to minimizing time, not the objective itself.

Hierarchical placement first respects expensive communication boundaries and then balances within faster domains. A globally ideal compute balance can be a poor placement if it sends each token's selected experts to many remote nodes. Measure both the rank load distribution and the number of distinct remote destinations per token. A replica can improve one while worsening the other.

Derivation: replication is a minimax allocation with integer constraints

Suppose expert e receives expected load λₑ and one replica sustains rate μₑ at the relevant batch shape. With rₑ replicas and perfect balancing, its utilization proxy is ρₑ=λₑ/(rₑμₑ). A synchronous layer waits for its slowest busy resource, so a first approximation is to minimize maxₑ ρₑ subject to Σₑrₑ=R and rₑ≥1. This ignores network and placement conflicts; those must be checked after allocation.

For a candidate maximum utilization τ, every expert needs at least ceil(λₑ/(τμₑ)) replicas, with a minimum of one. Thus τ is feasible exactly when the sum of these minima fits R in this simplified model. Bisection over τ solves the integer minimax allocation. If replicas were divisible and there were no minimum-one constraint, equalizing all λₑ/(rₑμₑ) gives rₑ proportional to λₑ/μₑ.

re,min⁡(τ)=max⁡(1,⌈λeτμe⌉)Feasible⁡(τ)  ⟺  ∑ere,min⁡(τ)≤R\begin{aligned}r_{e,\min}(\tau)&=\max\left(1,\left\lceil\frac{\lambda_e}{\tau\mu_e}\right\rceil\right)\\\operatorname{Feasible}(\tau)&\iff\sum_e r_{e,\min}(\tau)\le R\end{aligned}re,min​(τ)Feasible(τ)​=max(1,⌈τμe​λe​​⌉)⟺e∑​re,min​(τ)≤R​

This is a stronger statement than “replicate popular experts”: replica count depends on service cost as well as popularity. If a hot expert is already cheap, replicating an expensive moderate-load expert may reduce the layer maximum more.

A replica costs weight memory. If it displaces ΔM bytes of KV, it may reduce request concurrency or cause extra prefill. Placement can also route more activations across a slow link. Replication should therefore minimize a measured completion-time model under both memory and topology constraints. The minimax solution above is a baseline lower-level allocator, not an end-to-end theorem.

Exercise — Allocate six replicas

Three equally fast experts have loads (8,4,2), require at least one replica each, and have a total budget of six. Find an integer allocation minimizing maximum load per replica.

Show worked solution

Allocation (3,2,1) gives loads (8/3,2,2), so τ=8/3. Could τ be smaller? Expert 1 would need at least four replicas, expert 2 at least two, and expert 3 at least one, totaling seven. Therefore no smaller τ is feasible and (3,2,1) is optimal in the stated model. The continuous solution (24/7,12/7,6/7) violates the minimum-one constraint on expert 3 and is not executable as written.

7 · 2023–2025: offloading splits into several research problems

Problems and objectives. Experts may not fit in GPU memory even though each token activates only a few of them. This branch separates the questions of predicting future experts, choosing what to retain, moving weights versus activations, and accepting approximation; these mechanisms solve different causes of exposed miss latency.

7.1 Demand loading establishes the baseline

When the complete expert pool exceeds GPU memory, a common design keeps attention and other frequently used weights on the GPU, stores the expert pool in host memory, and caches selected experts on the GPU. A miss triggers weight transfer. This preserves the checkpoint if the right weights are fetched and computed, but the cache may thrash under a batch whose expert union approaches the full pool.

The useful metric is not hit rate alone. A small rarely used expert and a huge frequently used expert have different miss costs. A miss may be fully hidden by computation or lie directly on the token's critical path. Prefetching a correct expert too late is still a stall; prefetching it too early can evict another expert needed first. Report bytes moved, exposed transfer time, prediction precision/recall, and the distribution of stalls.

7.2 Pre-gated MoE: move the decision before the dependency

Core idea. Predict an upcoming expert choice early enough to begin fetching weights before the ordinary routing dependency would allow it. The extra lookahead requires an architectural or learned predictor contract, rather than being a transparent consequence of caching.

Ordinary gating needs the current layer's input state, so the selected weights may be unknown until immediately before they are used. Pre-gated MoE changes this dependency: a gate earlier in the execution predicts/selects experts for a later block, creating a window in which the system can load them. This is an algorithm–system co-design that requires the corresponding trained architecture. It should not be described as a lossless prefetch toggle for an arbitrary existing model. [11]

The blue selection path runs ahead of the green execution path. While the left block computes experts 0 and 2, its early decision initiates loading of the next block's experts 1 and 3. The optimization is possible because the selection deadline changed. In a conventional checkpoint, a heuristic predictor can create an analogous prefetch window, but wrong predictions require a fallback to the real gate; replacing that gate changes the model.

The governing inequality is simple: transfer time must fit inside available lookahead compute time, or only part of it is hidden. As GPUs accelerate the compute between decisions, the prefetch window can become shorter. Faster compute can therefore make an offloading design more transfer-bound even when nothing about PCIe changes. This is one reason bandwidth, scheduling, and architectural prediction need to be evaluated together.

7.3 SiDA-MoE: predict a batch's routing table outside its forward pass

Core idea. Train a predictor to produce a batch’s expert choices and scaling factors outside the main forward path, then use that table to orchestrate sparse execution. Because it substitutes for the original routing computation in the reported design, prediction quality is part of correctness.

SiDA's hash-building thread consumes an incoming batch and constructs a table describing expert choices and scaling factors across layers. An inference thread processes an earlier batch using its table, loading and offloading experts according to the predicted access pattern. For models with learned routers, the paper trains a lightweight predictor; its LSTM uses sparse attention over token embeddings, with truncated distillation of important router outputs plus a classification objective. [12]

The two threads have different jobs. On the right, the predictor prepares H_j for batch X_j and queues it. On the left, the inference path consumes H_i for X_i and uses it to manage which expert weights are on the GPU. The prediction includes more than a cache hint: the reported system removes the original routers from the inference forward path. Consequently, routing approximation and output quality are part of its algorithmic contract.

This distinction corrects an easy misreading. SiDA is not merely “LRU with better prefetch.” It changes how expert activation is obtained. Its accuracy, memory saving, and throughput must be reported together. Its batch-oriented setup also does not directly establish performance for every online autoregressive schedule, where future generated token identities are unavailable. The trained predictor's domain coverage and the workload used to build its supervision matter.

7.4 Fiddler: move the token to the weights

Core idea. For a cold expert serving few tokens, execute beside CPU-resident weights and move the small activations; for a resident or sufficiently busy expert, use the GPU. Profile the crossover so avoided weight traffic is weighed against slower host computation.

Fiddler notices that a decode miss often requires a huge weight tensor for very few token vectors. Instead of transferring that tensor to the GPU, execute the cold expert on the CPU and return its small output. For a hot expert already resident on the GPU, use the GPU directly. For a cold expert with enough tokens to amortize loading, transferring weights and computing on the GPU can again become preferable. [13]

The three cases are alternative execution paths for the same expert computation. In (a), the weights are already on the GPU. In (b), a miss moves weights to the GPU. In (c), the input activation moves to the CPU, where the weights remain, and the result moves back. The figure makes the unit of movement explicit; “offload” is too vague to distinguish these paths.

tGPU miss(n)≈Wexpertβlink+tGPU(n)tCPU(n)≈2ndsaβlink+thost expert(n)Choose the lower measured completion time, including overlap and queues.\begin{aligned}t_{\mathrm{GPU\ miss}}(n)&\approx\frac{W_{\mathrm{expert}}}{\beta_{\mathrm{link}}}+t_{\mathrm{GPU}}(n)\\t_{\mathrm{CPU}}(n)&\approx\frac{2nds_a}{\beta_{\mathrm{link}}}+t_{\mathrm{host\ expert}}(n)\\&\text{Choose the lower measured completion time, including overlap and queues.}\end{aligned}tGPU miss​(n)tCPU​(n)​≈βlink​Wexpert​​+tGPU​(n)≈βlink​2ndsa​​+thost expert​(n)Choose the lower measured completion time, including overlap and queues.​

Fiddler profiles the relationship between expert token count and the two execution times. It uses offline popularity estimates to keep useful experts resident and employs AVX512_BF16 CPU kernels for the uncompressed 16-bit model. For small n, avoided weight transfer can dominate; for long prefill or beam search, GPU batching gains change the choice. Its revised ICLR report evaluates uncompressed Mixtral-8×7B on single-GPU heterogeneous systems and reports different gains for single-batch generation, long prefill, and beam search. Those are three experiments, not one speedup that applies to every use case.

A practical extension of its reasoning is NUMA-aware placement. Host weights allocated on memory attached to the wrong CPU socket may cross an inter-socket link before reaching the executing core or GPU. CPU inference also competes with tokenization, scheduling, storage, and networking. Counting “unused CPU FLOPs” without accounting for host memory bandwidth can overstate the benefit.

Derivation: when moving activations beats moving weights

Use seconds, bytes, and tokens consistently. Let W be expert weight bytes, a be input-plus-output activation bytes per assigned token, β the effective transfer bandwidth, t₀ CPU/GPU-independent overhead, and let the measured compute paths be locally approximated by τC n and τG n for n tokens. For a GPU cache miss versus CPU execution:

Tmiss(n)=Wβ+τGnTCPU(n)=anβ+τCnTCPU(n)<Tmiss(n)  ⟺  n(τC−τG+aβ)<Wβ\begin{aligned}T_{\mathrm{miss}}(n)&=\frac W\beta+\tau_Gn\\T_{\mathrm{CPU}}(n)&=\frac{an}\beta+\tau_Cn\\T_{\mathrm{CPU}}(n)<T_{\mathrm{miss}}(n)&\iff n\left(\tau_C-\tau_G+\frac a\beta\right)<\frac W\beta\end{aligned}Tmiss​(n)TCPU​(n)TCPU​(n)<Tmiss​(n)​=βW​+τG​n=βan​+τC​n⟺n(τC​−τG​+βa​)<βW​​

If the bracket is positive, the crossing is n*=W/[β(τC−τG)+a]. Below n*, avoiding weight movement dominates; above n*, faster GPU execution can amortize the fetch. If the bracket is nonpositive, this simplified model predicts CPU preference for every n, signaling either an unusually slow GPU path or a model fit outside its useful range. Real GEMM rates depend strongly on n, so a piecewise measured model is preferable to extrapolation.

Now include residency. If the requested expert is on the GPU with probability h, expected GPU time becomes (1−h)W/β+τGn only under a simplified no-overlap model. Raising h lowers the crossing threshold. A prefetch may further hide part of W/β behind independent work, but then only the exposed transfer belongs in this inequality. Counting both a full transfer cost and a fully overlapped schedule would double-count the penalty.

Numerical scale. With W=350 MB, β=25 GB/s, a=16 KB/token, τC=0.20 ms/token and τG=0.01 ms/token, the miss costs 14 ms before compute. The CPU's extra per-token cost is 0.19064 ms, giving n*≈73.44. This is a teaching calculation; CPU bandwidth contention and GPU batch saturation can move the empirical crossover sharply.

Exercise — A 90% GPU hit rate

Use the preceding numerical model and h=0.9. Find the expected-cost crossover. Does this prove that all requests with fewer tokens should always run on the CPU?

Show worked solution

The expected exposed fetch cost is 0.1·14=1.4 ms. Therefore n*=1.4/0.19064≈7.34 tokens. No universal per-request decision follows from this expectation. On a known hit, GPU execution is faster in this model; on a known miss, the original 73.44 crossing applies. Observing actual residency is more informative than averaging over h.

7.5 MoE-Infinity: the access pattern belongs to a request

Core idea. Match a request’s partial layer-by-expert activation pattern to historical patterns to estimate upcoming expert use. Feed that request-conditioned prediction into both prefetch and retention decisions instead of relying only on global frequency or recency.

An LRU cache remembers recency, and a global-frequency cache remembers overall popularity. MoE-Infinity argues that neither captures the full sparse pattern of a particular generation request. It records expert activation matrices over layers and experts, maintaining both per-iteration and accumulated request information. It matches the current partial pattern to historical patterns and estimates future activation/reuse. Prefill and decode statistics are kept distinct. [24]

The matrix rows represent layers, not token positions. The observed partial activation matrix is matched against an activation-matrix collection. Similar historical patterns are aggregated into expected later activity; layer proximity then affects priority. The picture explains why a single scalar global frequency cannot express the same prediction: it loses which experts co-occur across one request's execution.

Follow the highlighted miss/hit decisions. LRU may evict a useful later expert merely because it was not accessed most recently. Global counting can retain a generally popular expert that does not fit this request. The request-conditioned prediction tries to retain and prefetch the experts likely to matter for the actual continuation. The example is illustrative; prediction quality must still be measured under changing task mixtures.

Prefetching and retention solve related but distinct questions. Prefetch asks “what will be needed soon enough to justify transfer now?” Retention asks “what is expensive to evict over a longer horizon?” Early-layer experts may deserve stronger residency because little prior computation is available to hide their misses. Later layers offer more lookahead. The latest paper's cache policy combines predicted reuse and layer information; it should not be reduced to “predict next expert.” The reference title and experiments changed across revisions, so the archived PDF is the evidence for this discussion.

7.6 MoE-Lightning: optimize an offline heterogeneous pipeline

Core idea. Coordinate CPU computation, GPU computation, and I/O as a throughput-oriented heterogeneous pipeline. Paged weight transfers and a hierarchy-aware cost model help prevent large transfers from blocking smaller urgent dependencies.

MoE-Lightning targets throughput-oriented batch workloads on memory-constrained GPUs. Its CGOPipe schedule coordinates CPU work, GPU work, and I/O, using paged weights to avoid a large monolithic transfer monopolizing the link. A hierarchical roofline model accounts for several memory/compute boundaries when choosing placement and scheduling policies. [25]

The important scheduling hazard is head-of-line blocking on I/O: a large weight transfer can delay a much smaller activation that the GPU urgently needs. Splitting transfer units permits more useful ordering and overlap. Weight and KV policies must be chosen together because both compete for GPU memory and host bandwidth. The system's large throughput gain on a T4 with Mixtral is evidence about offline batched execution, not an interactive TPOT guarantee.

7.7 HOBBIT and Lynx: explicitly approximate the computation

Core idea. HOBBIT varies precision and potentially skips low-importance contributions to reduce miss cost; Lynx remaps lower-affinity assignments to reduce the batch’s distinct expert set. Both trade some numerical or routing fidelity for lower serving cost and therefore need quality measurements alongside speed.

HOBBIT keeps multiple precision versions and chooses cheaper loading for less important cache-miss experts, alongside adaptive prefetch and a richer caching policy. Its runtime importance estimate uses routing information and a proxy for the expert contribution; the design can also skip extremely low-importance contributions. This changes numerical or routing behavior and must be evaluated on quality as well as time. A cache hit on a high-precision copy and a miss served with a low-precision copy need not compute exactly the same output. [26]

Lynx attacks the batch-union problem directly. Its AffinityBinning machinery identifies lower-affinity assignments and remaps them to reduce the set of distinct experts invoked by the batch. This increases reuse of a smaller weight set. It is categorically different from choosing between two identical physical replicas: a logical expert assignment can change. The latest archived version evaluates several model families and reports up to 1.30× lower latency under its workloads; the original preprint's headline and method presentation differ. Version-specific figures should not be mixed into one result. [27]

The mechanism suggests the right stress tests: tasks where rare experts carry decisive knowledge, different languages and domains, changed batch composition, long reasoning trajectories, and tokens with a large gap between their preferred expert and alternatives. Small average quality loss is compatible with concentrated failure on a narrow domain. Such systems can be useful, but their service contract includes an accuracy budget.

8 · 2024–2026: fine-grained experts reshape the serving architecture

Problems and objectives. Finer expert specialization can improve model capacity at similar activated FLOPs, but it creates smaller GEMMs, more routing metadata, and more potential destinations. Architecture and serving now have to coordinate expert granularity, shared computation, destination constraints, and dispatch kernels.

8.1 DeepSeekMoE: more combinations at the same activated width

Core idea. Split routed experts into finer units and reserve shared experts for broadly useful computation. More selective combinations can improve specialization at comparable activated width, while increasing the number of expert groups the serving system must handle.

DeepSeekMoE identifies two sources of inefficient expert capacity: coarse experts entangle different kinds of knowledge, and multiple routed experts redundantly learn common information. Its fine-grained segmentation divides each expert's intermediate width into smaller units, expands the expert count, and increases the number selected so the total activated width remains comparable. Shared experts capture broadly useful computation, while routed experts specialize. [5]

Hold parameter count and activated width fixed while reading left to right. The conventional top-2 architecture becomes a larger set of half-width experts with top-4 selection. The final panel dedicates one small expert to shared computation and selects three routed experts. The diagram does not claim that an arbitrary trained coarse expert can be split after training with no quality change; it illustrates the architecture used for learning specialization.

(E′,h′,k′)=(mE,h/m,mk)Ptotal′=(mE)3dhm=3EdhFactive′=(mk)6dhm=6kdhNsubsets′=(mEmk),Nsubsets=(Ek)\begin{aligned}(E',h',k')&=(mE,h/m,mk)\\P_{\mathrm{total}}'&=(mE)3d\frac hm=3Edh\\F_{\mathrm{active}}'&=(mk)6d\frac hm=6kdh\\N_{\mathrm{subsets}}'&=\binom{mE}{mk},\quad N_{\mathrm{subsets}}=\binom Ek\end{aligned}(E′,h′,k′)Ptotal′​Factive′​Nsubsets′​​=(mE,h/m,mk)=(mE)3dmh​=3Edh=(mk)6dmh​=6kdh=(mkmE​),Nsubsets​=(kE​)​

The combinatorial count illustrates flexibility; it is not a theorem about independent semantic concepts or output quality. The serving consequences are concrete: more routing indices, more expert groups, narrower matrices, and potentially more destinations per token. An architectural quality improvement at equal FLOPs can therefore require better grouped kernels and communication to become an equal-latency improvement.

Shared experts also complicate simplistic sparsity ratios. They consume arithmetic every token but offer predictable dense work that can sometimes overlap routed communication. They may be replicated differently from routed experts. A cost model should separate shared and routed storage, compute, and placement.

Derivation: fine-grained experts conserve arithmetic but increase other costs

Start with E experts of intermediate width h and select k per token. Ignoring biases, a gated FFN has three d×h matrices. Total expert parameters are 3Edh and selected parameters per token are 3kdh. Split each expert's width by m while multiplying the expert count and selected count by m:

E′=mE,h′=hm,k′=mkPtotal′=3(mE)dhm=3EdhPactive′=3(mk)dhm=3kdh\begin{aligned}E'&=mE,\quad h'=\frac hm,\quad k'=mk\\P_{\mathrm{total}}'&=3(mE)d\frac hm=3Edh\\P_{\mathrm{active}}'&=3(mk)d\frac hm=3kdh\end{aligned}E′Ptotal′​Pactive′​​=mE,h′=mh​,k′=mk=3(mE)dmh​=3Edh=3(mk)dmh​=3kdh​

The arithmetic count is conserved in this idealized construction, but the number of token–expert assignments becomes m times larger. Each assignment may carry a d-dimensional token vector, so naive dispatch payload grows with mkd even though expert GEMM FLOPs stay fixed. Fine-grained expert routing can therefore trade more flexible specialization for more communication, smaller matrix problems, and larger routing metadata.

The number of possible selected sets changes from C(E,k) to C(mE,mk). This counts combinatorial choices, not independently learnable functions or guaranteed model quality. Experts can be redundant, the router may use only a small subset of combinations, and training can fail to exploit the larger choice space. Shared experts further change the parameter and FLOP ledger: count their always-active width separately before comparing two models.

A topology-aware router can reduce remote-node fanout by concentrating selected experts within a limited number of nodes. That creates another trade: constrained placement may reduce network traffic while changing which expert combinations are available. It cannot be justified solely by the conserved parameter calculation above.

8.2 DeepSeek-V3: constrain expensive communication without discarding specialization

Core idea. Coordinate fine-grained expert routing with limits on expensive destinations and mechanisms for balancing expert use. The aim is to retain specialization while keeping communication and load skew compatible with large-scale execution.

The V3 report combines fine-grained experts, shared experts, node-limited routing, and load balancing. Node-limited routing constrains how many nodes a token must visit, addressing the number of expensive cross-node destinations. This is a model/system choice designed into the recipe. It is not equivalent to placing arbitrary selected experts on any convenient nearby rank after the fact. [6]

Its auxiliary-loss-free balancing approach adjusts selection biases based on recent expert load while using the original affinity values for the selected experts' combination weights. The distinction between the score used to select and the value used to weight matters: inserting the balancing bias into both changes the function. The report also includes a small sequence-wise auxiliary objective; the phrase “auxiliary-loss-free” should not be expanded into a claim that every balancing-related auxiliary term disappeared.

At deployment, redundant expert copies can balance physical work without retraining the logical router. Prefill and decode use different parallelism and scheduling because prefill supplies large matrices while decode must meet low latency with smaller batches. The report's deployment design, DeepEP transport, DeepGEMM kernels, and EPLB placement address different layers of this stack; none individually explains the whole service throughput.

8.3 DeepEP: communication is a GPU workload too

Core idea. Implement dispatch and combine as GPU communication workloads tailored to expert-parallel execution and the machine’s link hierarchy. Efficient transport must preserve token identity, routing weights, and destination layout while sharing GPU resources with compute.

Dispatch/combine must move token payloads, preserve routing metadata, and deliver an expert-friendly layout. The legacy DeepEP design separates high-throughput paths from low-latency decode paths and exploits NVLink/RDMA asymmetry. Its FP8 dispatch and BF16 combine examples have different payload widths, so a single “communication precision” label is insufficient. [15]

Communication kernels can occupy SMs that would otherwise run expert GEMMs. Thus a transport with slightly lower standalone bandwidth may yield a faster complete layer if it leaves more compute resources available or enables finer overlap. Conversely, a transfer that appears hidden in a trace may slow the overlapped GEMM through resource contention. Measure the overlapped pair, not merely their separate runtimes.

The September 2026 V2 documentation describes a different NCCL Gin backend, JIT compilation, and a unified ElasticBuffer interface. It also explicitly states that the old zero-SM low-latency RDMA EP mode is no longer supported. Preserve that version boundary when translating a 2025 benchmark or integration example. Its reported “logical bandwidth” can include local-rank traffic, so it must not be read as the number of physical bytes crossing one NIC. [14]

8.4 What a correct dispatch/combine integration must preserve

A compact implementation sketch makes the semantics clear. Production kernels fuse several of these steps, but fusion does not remove their obligations.

scores, logical_experts, weights = route(hidden)
physical_destinations = replica_map(logical_experts, placement_version)
layout = count_and_prefix_sum(physical_destinations)
packed, reverse_map = pack(hidden, destinations, token_ids)
received, handle = dispatch(packed, layout)
expert_outputs = grouped_experts(received, per_expert_counts, scales)
returned = combine(expert_outputs, handle)
output = weighted_scatter_add(returned, reverse_map, weights)

The handle needs enough information to reverse the route. Top-k weights must be applied exactly once. Quantization scales must travel with the intended values and grouping. Padding lanes must contribute zero. A placement update must not cause one stage to interpret an old logical-to-physical map using a new expert copy. Routing metadata can only be reused when its validity conditions hold; similar batch shape is not proof of identical routing.

These details explain why communication and kernels are co-designed. Dispatch output layout determines expert GEMM input layout; GEMM output partitioning determines when combine can begin. Optimizing one boundary while forcing an extra full-tensor permutation at the next can lose the apparent gain.

9 · 2025–2026: separate attention from experts

Problems and objectives. Attention and experts prefer different batch sizes and resource layouts, making a single colocated execution plan inefficient. This branch separates their workers, then asks whether batching and pipelining gains can repay the new activation-transfer boundary without worsening token latency.

9.1 MegaScale-Infer identifies incompatible batch preferences

Core idea. Place attention and expert computation on separate worker pools so each can use a suitable parallelism and batching strategy. Transfer activations between them and pipeline microbatches to amortize expert execution without exposing the entire new boundary on the critical path.

Attention keeps request-specific KV state and processes sequences with different context lengths. Routed experts are largely stateless functions of the current token representations and can aggregate assignments from many request groups. In a monolithic deployment, both modules inherit a coupled GPU allocation and batch structure. MegaScale-Infer separates them onto attention workers and expert workers so each side can use a more suitable parallelism and hardware allocation. [28]

This figure is a conceptual utilization argument. The red FFN curve benefits strongly from larger batches; the attention curve has a different shape. In an MoE, each expert receives only part of the global batch, delaying the point at which its matrix operations become efficient. Disaggregation lets the expert pool see aggregated work from multiple attention replicas. The dashed improvements in the third panel explain the design hypothesis; they are not a measured throughput curve for every hardware configuration.

The separation is within every transformer layer. M attention replicas own attention parameters and KV state, while N expert workers own the expert pool. M2N and N2M transfers move activations and outputs between them. Each side can still use tensor parallelism internally. This is different from prefill/decode separation, which assigns different phases of a request to different workers while transferring its KV state at the phase boundary. The two forms of disaggregation can be combined, but they solve different imbalances.

9.2 Ping-pong microbatches hide the new boundary

Disaggregation creates an additional dependency: attention must send activations to the expert pool and receive expert outputs before the request can enter the next layer. MegaScale-Infer pipelines several microbatches across these modules. While experts process one microbatch, attention workers process another; activations shuttle between the pools. The schedule must contain enough independent microbatches to cover communication and avoid idle gaps.

Read horizontally for time and vertically for resources. Each labeled box identifies a microbatch and layer. Red arrows are cross-layer dependencies for the same microbatch. Attention, attention-to-expert communication, expert computation, and expert-to-attention communication have separate rows. Their offset is what makes simultaneous useful work possible. Increasing microbatch count provides more overlap opportunities but also changes individual matrix sizes and the time a request spends circulating through the pipeline.

The paper models attention time T_a, expert time T_e, and transfer time T_c. The useful intuition is that a filled pipeline is limited by its slowest service stage, while startup/drain and request-level dependencies remain. An idealized lower bound is max(T_a,T_e,T_c) per scheduled unit when communication directions and resources allow that overlap. Real constraints include link sharing, finite buffers, batch formation delay, and asymmetric pool capacity; the exact schedule's formulas should not be replaced by an unconditional max bound.

Derivation: a pipeline hides time only when another stage supplies enough work

Model a stream of m independent microbatches through two ordered stages with service times a and e. Assume each stage has its own resources, unlimited intermediate buffering, and no cross-microbatch dependency. The first result needs a+e. Every subsequent result can emerge at intervals max(a,e): the slower stage sets the steady-state cadence.

Tserial=m(a+e)Tpipeline=a+e+(m−1)max⁡(a,e)S=m(a+e)a+e+(m−1)max⁡(a,e)lim⁡m→∞S=a+emax⁡(a,e)≤2\begin{aligned}T_{\mathrm{serial}}&=m(a+e)\\T_{\mathrm{pipeline}}&=a+e+(m-1)\max(a,e)\\S&=\frac{m(a+e)}{a+e+(m-1)\max(a,e)}\\\lim_{m\to\infty}S&=\frac{a+e}{\max(a,e)}\le2\end{aligned}Tserial​Tpipeline​Sm→∞lim​S​=m(a+e)=a+e+(m−1)max(a,e)=a+e+(m−1)max(a,e)m(a+e)​=max(a,e)a+e​≤2​

The upper bound of two is reached only for balanced a=e with a long stream. For a=2 ms, e=8 ms, the asymptotic bound is only 1.25×, however many microbatches are added. A communication stage c can be included as a third independently resourced stage, yielding fill a+c+e and cadence max(a,c,e). If communication shares SMs or HBM with computation, independence fails and those ideal maxima can be unattainable.

In a multilayer MoE, the same request cannot start attention at layer ℓ+1 before its layer-ℓ expert result returns. Interleaving other microbatches creates the work that fills this gap. Batching therefore improves aggregate utilization while potentially increasing the residence time of any one request. To optimize serving, derive both throughput and per-request latency from the actual schedule instead of treating pipeline speedup as an automatic ITL improvement.

Exercise — Four microbatches through unequal stages

For a=3 ms, e=5 ms and m=4, compute serial time, ideal pipeline time and speedup. If a new independent 7 ms communication stage is introduced, what is the new ideal total?

Show worked solution

Serial two-stage time is 4·8=32 ms. Pipeline time is 3+5+3·5=23 ms, a 32/23≈1.39× improvement. With a separate 7 ms communication stage, fill time is 15 ms and cadence is 7 ms, so total is 15+3·7=36 ms. Overlap does not make the extra boundary free: even the ideal three-stage pipeline is now slower than the original serial two-stage execution.

9.3 The M2N library is part of the method

A generic collective interface may assume a fixed participant group and synchronized progression. Disaggregated attention/expert traffic is a many-to-many exchange with potentially different numbers of senders and receivers, changing token destinations, and latency-sensitive small messages. MegaScale-Infer's M2N path avoids unnecessary host copies, group-management overhead, and synchronization in this specific pattern. The sender/receiver protocol and pipeline architecture are co-designed. [28]

This is why simply placing attention on GPU A and experts on GPU B is not a reproduction of the paper. The extra communication must be implemented efficiently, and enough work must overlap it. Heterogeneous hardware can help when the two modules favor different memory/compute ratios, but cheaper expert hardware can also become the bottleneck if grouped matrices are too small or its interconnect is weak.

9.4 Read the results as a latency–throughput comparison

The three panels must be read together. Left: normalized decoding throughput per GPU. Middle: mean time between tokens for the corresponding configuration. Right: end-to-end throughput including prefill. The models are Mixtral-8×22B, DBRX, and a scaled MoE; the comparison is on the paper's NVIDIA Ampere configuration. A larger left bar with a worse middle bar is a tradeoff, not an unqualified win. Normalizing by GPU count is essential because a disaggregated design uses separate pools, all of which contribute to cost.

The paper reports up to 1.90× higher per-GPU decoding throughput and up to 1.18× higher end-to-end throughput including prefill in its homogeneous experiments and evaluates heterogeneous placements separately. Those results support the mechanism under the tested batch and hardware regimes. They do not imply that one interactive request benefits from a remote expert service. Small deployments may lose more to transport than they gain from aggregation, and an already well-balanced monolithic service may have less headroom.

9.5 Wide EP and fault isolation extend the design space

Wide expert parallelism aggregates work over a larger expert domain while attention can remain distributed across request groups. Its appeal is larger useful expert batches and distributed weight capacity; its costs are a wider synchronization domain, more network pressure, and the need for load balancing. The vLLM wide-EP engineering report should be read as a complete runtime configuration, including its request lengths, precision, and latency targets. A per-H200 throughput headline is not a universal property of the checkpoint. [18]

Tarragon studies another consequence of disaggregation: different state and failure behavior on the two sides. Attention workers own request-specific KV; expert workers can often recover from replicas of comparatively static parameters. It combines incremental KV checkpointing, shadow experts, and a reconfigurable data path to limit the effect of a failed worker. Its reported reduction in failure-induced stalls—from roughly 64 seconds to 0.3–0.4 seconds in the study—is a resilience result, not a normal-operation speedup. [29]

Fault handling is relevant to the optimization objective because a fast average service with occasional fleet-wide stalls can have poor goodput. Replication used for load balance and replication used for recovery may share storage, but they require different guarantees: a hot replica improves normal throughput; a recovery replica must be reachable and consistent when the original failure domain is unavailable.

10 · A chronological map with the mechanisms kept separate

Period and landmarkCore problem exposedMethod family and variantsWhat the next generation inherits
2017 sparse gating; 2020 GShard; 2021 SwitchGrow capacity without dense per-token computeNoisy/top-k gates; distributed top-2; top-1; capacity and balancingDynamic destinations, overflow, and quality–balance tension
2021 FastMoE; 2022 FasterMoE/DeepSpeed-MoESparse model does not execute efficiently across devicesExpert parallelism, slicing, shadowing, hierarchical communicationParallel dimensions need different layouts and schedules
2022–2023 Tutel/MegaBlocksUnequal expert batches conflict with regular kernelsAdaptive parallelism/pipelining; block-sparse dropless executionShape-aware kernels and cheap routing metadata
2023 LinaCollective contention and inference popularity skewPrioritize urgent exchanges; predict load and place replicasOptimize the slowest rank and migration timescale
2023–2025 Pre-gated/SiDA/Fiddler/MoE-InfinityFull expert pool does not fit HBMEarlier selection, predictive tables, host compute, request-conditioned cachingPrediction validity, miss critical paths, and CPU–GPU tradeoffs
2024 MoE-Lightning/HOBBIT/LynxThroughput or weight traffic still limits offloaded/batched serviceHeterogeneous pipelines; dynamic precision; batch-aware remappingExplicit quality budgets and distinct workload objectives
2024–2026 DeepSeekMoE/V3, DeepGEMM/DeepEP/EPLBFiner experts amplify kernel, topology, and placement complexityShared experts, node limits, grouped kernels, specialized transfer, replicasJoint architecture and runtime design
2025–2026 MegaScale-Infer/TarragonAttention and experts need different resources and failure domainsAttention/expert disaggregation; ping-pong pipelines; selective recoveryCapacity, latency, and resilience become fleet-level objectives

The table is a set of overlapping lineages, not a claim that each new paper replaces its predecessors. A modern runtime can combine expert replication, grouped GEMM, low-precision dispatch, prefill/decode separation, and request-aware admission. An offloaded workstation can combine quantized weights, host execution, caching, and prefetch. What matters is whether their assumptions and data layouts compose.
