There is no defensible single ranking across this table. The professional comparison is a Pareto surface over quality, latency, throughput, memory, and total cost. For example, HOBBIT and an exact BF16 host-execution path solve different quality contracts; MegaBlocks and MegaScale-Infer measure different phases; a T4 offload result and an H200 fleet result use different resource envelopes.

A controlled serving experiment

Freeze the checkpoint, tokenizer, routing semantics, weight/KV precision, hardware allocation, and request trace. Record prompt/output length distributions, arrival process, task domains, prefix-cache behavior, and warmup. Sweep offered load and batch limits rather than choosing one favorable point. Report p50/p95/p99 TTFT and TPOT, goodput, peak memory, per-expert token histograms, dispatch/combine bytes, expert-cache misses, and exposed transfer time.

Then isolate components: unchanged placement with a new kernel; unchanged kernel with replica balancing; unchanged model with offload policy changes; and separately any altered precision or routing. Compare the complete allocation, including attention workers, expert workers, standby replicas, host CPUs, and memory. An apparent per-active-GPU gain can vanish when idle reserved capacity is counted.

For routing-changing methods, use several task domains and long generations, with paired runs and enough trials to reveal variance. Inspect failure concentration, not just the mean. For exact execution changes, compare outputs or logits under a documented numerical tolerance; parallel reduction order can change floating-point results without changing the intended model. Do not demand bitwise identity and simultaneously change arithmetic precision.

12 · Derivations and practical decisions

12.1 Why a higher cache hit rate can lose

Let expert e have miss probability m_e, miss transfer cost c_e, and hidden fraction h_e. A first approximation to exposed miss cost is Σ_e m_e c_e(1−h_e), evaluated along the request's dependencies. Maximizing unweighted hit count optimizes Σ_e(1−m_e), a different objective. Retaining an expert whose misses are already fully hidden can be less valuable than retaining one modestly frequent expert that stalls the first layer.

This suggests a cost-aware priority, but not an infallible policy. Predicting h_e requires the current pipeline, link queues, and future batch structure. When traffic changes, a previously excellent prefetch may become harmful. Keep a demand path that guarantees correct execution and instrument why each miss became visible.

12.2 When replication stops helping

Suppose a hot expert gets λ assignments and r replicas. Ignoring nonlinearity, per-replica load falls as λ/r. But memory grows as rW, each replica may read its own weights, and smaller local n_e can reduce arithmetic intensity. If KV capacity limits the batch, added weight replicas can lower the very λ that made replication useful. The best r is therefore a coupled memory/shape/network decision.

A simple analytical lower bound also explains why average load is insufficient. If device capacity is identical and total expert work is F_total, ideal compute time is at least F_total/(pC). Actual placement adds a skew factor and kernel inefficiency. Replication can reduce skew, but cannot beat the capacity bound or eliminate mandatory attention and transport work. Once a different stage dominates, further replicas have diminishing benefit.

12.3 Amdahl's law applies to every attractive kernel result

If fraction f of a decode step is expert computation and a new kernel accelerates that portion by s, the ideal end-to-end speedup is 1/[(1−f)+f/s]. If f=0.4 and s=2, the bound is only 1.25× before new overhead. At long context, attention may dominate; under cross-node EP, transport may dominate; on a workstation, host misses may dominate. Measure f at the actual workload point rather than importing it from another paper.

12.4 Decision guide

Observed bottleneckMost direct methods to investigateMeasurement that decides
Expert weights do not fit HBMQuantization, host caching, Fiddler-style CPU execution, MoE-Infinity, offline MoE-LightningQuality, miss bytes, PCIe/DRAM time, interactive versus batch objective
Many tiny expert GEMMsGrouped/masked kernels, larger useful expert batches, appropriate EP degreen_e distribution, padding ratio, launch time, effective FLOP/s
A few ranks dominate every stepEPLB/replication, better placement, Lina-style predictionSlowest-rank trace and migration amortization
All-to-all stalls despite little dataLow-latency transport, fewer synchronization points, localityMessage size, RTT, SM occupation, number of destinations
Large transfers dominateHierarchical dispatch, low-precision wire formats, overlapPhysical link bytes and accuracy after communication conversion
Attention and expert utilization divergeIndependent parallelism, attention/expert or prefill/decode separationPool utilization, transfer overhead, end-to-end SLO goodput
Weight union erases sparse traffic savingsLarger reuse per expert; quality-budgeted Lynx-like remappingDistinct experts per batch and domain-specific quality

The open problems follow directly: predicting load under changing traffic without expensive migration; scheduling expert work across requests without sacrificing latency; quantifying the quality effect of adaptive precision/routing; coordinating expert and KV memory policies; and preserving performance during failures. A strong new system contribution explains which bottleneck it removes, measures the new bottleneck it exposes, and shows the range of workloads over which the trade is worthwhile.

Check your understanding

1. Derive the distinct-expert expectation for E=64, k=8, and B=1, 8, 64. Explain why the same activated parameter count can correspond to different weight traffic per output token.

2. An expert has 352 MB of BF16 weights and receives two tokens. Compare transfer volume for weight offloading and CPU execution. Then explain why increasing its token batch can reverse the runtime preference.

3. A replica policy halves the worst expert load but reduces available KV memory by 20%. Construct a case in which goodput falls. Which measurements distinguish this from a broken kernel?

4. In the MegaScale-Infer pipeline, identify the dependency that prevents the same microbatch's next attention layer from starting early. Explain which independent microbatch can occupy the resource in the meantime.

5. Classify each change as exact execution, numerical approximation, routing approximation, or a newly trained architecture: expert replica selection, FP8 dispatch, HOBBIT low-precision misses, Lynx remapping, Pre-gated MoE, and DeepSeekMoE segmentation. State the evaluation contract for each.

References & reading route

Primary papers and official technical documents. Dates identify first reports or publication, not a claim of independent reproduction. Numerical results retain their original conditions.

  1. Outrageously Large Neural Networks: The Sparsely-Gated Mixture-of-Experts Layer. 2017. Conditional computation and noisy top-k routing.
  2. GShard: Scaling Giant Models with Conditional Computation and Automatic Sharding. 2020. Distributed top-2 MoE and capacity constraints.
  3. Switch Transformers. 2021. Top-1 routing, stability, and capacity.
  4. Mixtral of Experts. 2024. Eight experts and two selected experts per sparse layer.
  5. DeepSeekMoE: Towards Ultimate Expert Specialization in Mixture-of-Experts Language Models. 2024. Fine-grained and shared experts.
  6. DeepSeek-V3 Technical Report. 2024/2025. Routing, redundant experts, and deployment architecture; §§2–3.
  7. DeepSpeed-MoE: Advancing Mixture-of-Experts Inference and Training. 2022. Parallelism, inference kernels, and compression.
  8. Tutel: Adaptive Mixture-of-Experts at Scale. 2022/2023. Adaptive parallelism and pipelining.
  9. MegaBlocks: Efficient Sparse Training with Mixture-of-Experts. 2022/2023. Dropless block-sparse computation; training evidence.
  10. Accelerating Distributed MoE Training and Inference with Lina. USENIX ATC 2023. All-to-all scheduling and expert popularity.
  11. Pre-gated MoE: An Algorithm-System Co-Design for Fast and Scalable Mixture-of-Expert Inference. 2023. Predict earlier to enable expert preloading; architecture changes.
  12. SiDA-MoE: Sparsity-Inspired Data-Aware Serving. 2023. Expert caching and data-aware offloading.
  13. Fiddler: CPU-GPU Orchestration for Fast Inference of Mixture-of-Experts Models. 2024. Execute cold experts on CPUs to avoid moving large weights.
  14. DeepEP: expert-parallel communication library. Official repository, accessed September 2026. APIs are version-dependent; V2 differs from legacy V1.
  15. DeepEP legacy V1 design and benchmark documentation. 2025 architecture: throughput dispatch/combine and low-latency decode paths.
  16. DeepGEMM: BLAS kernels for dense and MoE computation. Official code. Contiguous and masked grouped-GEMM interfaces.
  17. Expert Parallelism Load Balancer. Official code. Replicate and place experts using estimated loads.
  18. vLLM Large Scale Serving: DeepSeek at 2.2k tok/s/H200 with Wide-EP. December 2025 engineering report. Conditions and complete configuration are essential to interpret the headline.
  19. FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness. 2022. Attention IO is a separate bottleneck from expert dispatch.
  20. DistServe: Disaggregating Prefill and Decoding for Goodput-optimized LLM Serving. 2024. SLO-aware phase separation; not an MoE-only method.
  21. FastMoE: A Fast Mixture-of-Expert Training System (2021). General GPU expert-parallel training implementation.
  22. FasterMoE: Modeling and Optimizing Training of Large-Scale Dynamic Pre-Trained Models (PPoPP 2022). Shadowing, fine-grained scheduling and congestion-aware routing; training evidence.
  23. Mixture-of-Experts with Expert Choice Routing (2022). Experts choose token buckets; variable number of experts per token.
  24. MoE-Infinity: Efficient MoE Inference on Personal Machines with Sparsity-Aware Expert Cache. 2024 initial preprint; archived current PDF uses the revised title and request-level activation matrix/cache analysis.
  25. MoE-Lightning: High-Throughput MoE Inference on Memory-constrained GPUs (2024). Offline throughput objective; CGOPipe, paged weights, hierarchical roofline.
  26. HOBBIT: A Mixed Precision Expert Offloading System for Fast MoE Inference (2024). Dynamic precision, importance estimation, prefetching and caching.
  27. LYNX: Enabling Efficient MoE Inference Through Dynamic Batch-Aware Expert Selection. 2024 initial preprint, revised through 2026. Guide uses the locally archived revision reporting up to 1.30× lower latency, with AffinityBinning.
  28. MegaScale-Infer: Serving Mixture-of-Experts at Scale with Disaggregated Expert Parallelism (2025). Attention/expert separation, ping-pong pipeline, M2N transport; original architecture and benchmark figures.
  29. Making MoE-based LLM Inference Resilient with TARRAGON (2026). Stateful attention workers and stateless expert recovery; failure-induced stall comparisons.
